patient.setting: GP surgery, then same-day eye casualty

background: Seropositive rheumatoid arthritis for 12 years, on methotrexate

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with a red eye in a patient with rheumatoid arthritis or vasculitis: severe pain worse on eye movement and failure to blanch with phenylephrine point to scleritis over episcleritis.

Globe is **tender** through the closed lid.

steps.lead: Fatima has the full picture: **severe pain worse on eye movement**, violet hue, tenderness, photophobia, reduced vision and pain radiating to the jaw.

steps.q: Which single feature best separates Fatima's scleritis from episcleritis?
steps.r: Scleritis pain is **severe and worse with eye movement**. Episcleritis is mild, with watering, and movement does not worsen it.

steps.q: The GP suspects scleritis. What is the most appropriate first step?
o: Chloramphenicol drops and review in 1 week
Topical steroid drops from the GP
steps.r: Scleritis is an **ophthalmological emergency**: same-day specialist assessment. GPs should not start topical steroids for a red eye.

steps.text: The **autoimmune screen** (RF, anti-CCP, ANCA, ANA) matters: about half of scleritis is linked to systemic disease, and finding it changes treatment.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?': same-day ophthalmology first, then oral NSAIDs for mild disease and systemic steroids (oral prednisolone or IV methylprednisolone) for severe or necrotising disease.

steps.lead: The GP's job for Fatima is one phone call: **same-day ophthalmology**, because scleritis threatens sight.

steps.q: In eye casualty Fatima has diffuse anterior scleritis, no necrosis. What is first treatment?
steps.r: Milder, non-necrotising scleritis starts with a **systemic NSAID** such as flurbiprofen 100 mg TDS. Topical drops do not reach the deep sclera.

points: Slit lamp: a new **avascular patch** in the sclera.

steps.title: Scleritis treatment ladder
nodes: Severe or NSAID failure → oral prednisolone

visual.caption: Little change on NSAIDs alone; pain and ESR fall once steroids start on day 7.

steps.lead: Fatima's care follows the **Royal College of Ophthalmologists** guidance and **NICE CKS Red eye**: urgent referral, then specialist-led treatment.

steps.text: Never treat suspected scleritis with **topical steroids alone** in primary care. It needs systemic treatment and an ophthalmologist.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: why phenylephrine does not blanch scleritis (deep plexus), why rheumatoid arthritis causes scleromalacia and perforation, or the type of inflammation involved.

steps.lead: Fatima's scleritis is an **extra-articular** feature of her RA: a granulomatous, **T-cell mediated** infiltrate in the sclera.
Her sclera is rigid and has little blood supply, so swelling **stretches the nerve-rich episclera**: that is why her pain is 9/10.
Phenylephrine constricts **superficial** vessels only. Fatima's inflammation is in the **deep vascular plexus**, so the redness stays.

steps.title: From RA to globe rupture
steps.caption: This is why necrotising scleritis needs pulsed steroids fast.

steps.lead: Fatima's avascular patch was early **necrosis**: left alone, it can thin into **scleromalacia** and rupture.

steps.q: Why did phenylephrine fail to blanch Fatima's eye?
steps.r: Scleritis involves the **deeper vascular plexus**; phenylephrine only blanches superficial episcleral and conjunctival vessels.

steps.text: **Scleromalacia perforans** is the painless, necrotising variant classically seen in long-standing **rheumatoid arthritis**.

mcq.q: Which feature most reliably distinguishes scleritis from episcleritis?
mcq.r: Scleritis pain is **worse with eye movement**; episcleritis pain is not.

mcq.q: Which condition is most associated with scleritis?
mcq.r: RA, vasculitis and SLE. **Ulcerative colitis** is the classic association of episcleritis.

mcq.q: What happens when phenylephrine is put in a scleritis eye?
mcq.r: Deep scleral vessels **do not blanch**; episcleral redness does.

mcq.q: Which is a recognised complication of scleritis?
mcq.r: Vision loss, **scleral thinning** and rarely **globe rupture**.

mcq.q: What is the first-line step for suspected scleritis?
mcq.r: It is an **ophthalmological emergency**: same-day assessment.

mcq.q: Which bloods are sent in scleritis?
mcq.r: **ESR/CRP and an autoimmune screen** look for the systemic cause.

mcq.q: Which drug is used for mild scleritis?
mcq.r: Systemic NSAID: ibuprofen or **flurbiprofen 100 mg TDS**.

mcq.q: What is used for severe scleritis?
mcq.r: Systemic steroids: oral prednisolone or pulsed **IV methylprednisolone**.

mcq.q: What type of infiltrate is seen in scleritis?
mcq.r: A **granulomatous, T-cell mediated** infiltrate within the sclera.

mcq.q: Why is scleritis pain so severe?
mcq.r: The sclera is **rigid and relatively avascular**; swelling stretches the nerve-rich episclera.

glossary.Scleritis: Inflammation of the sclera, the tough white outer coat of the eye; painful and sight-threatening.
glossary.Episcleritis: Mild, usually self-limiting inflammation of the thin layer over the sclera; not worse on eye movement.
glossary.sclera: The tough white outer wall of the eyeball.
glossary.episclera: The thin, nerve-rich vascular layer between the conjunctiva and the sclera.
glossary.Phenylephrine: Alpha-agonist eye drop that constricts superficial vessels; blanches episcleritis but not scleritis.
glossary.blanching: Whitening of a red area when its vessels constrict or are pressed.
glossary.Scleromalacia: Thinning and softening of the sclera, which can progress to perforation.
glossary.scleromalacia perforans: Painless necrotising scleritis without inflammation, classically in long-standing rheumatoid arthritis.
glossary.necrotising: Causing tissue death; necrotising scleritis is the most severe form.
glossary.globe rupture: A full-thickness break in the wall of the eyeball.
glossary.Photophobia: Pain or discomfort caused by light.
glossary.bulbar injection: Redness of the conjunctiva over the eyeball itself, rather than inside the lids.
glossary.Rheumatoid arthritis: Autoimmune inflammatory arthritis of small joints; the commonest cause of scleritis.
glossary.SLE: Systemic lupus erythematosus, a multisystem autoimmune disease with ANA antibodies.
glossary.vasculitis: Inflammation of blood vessel walls, causing narrowing, ischaemia or bleeding.
glossary.GPA: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis, an ANCA-positive small-vessel vasculitis that can cause scleritis.
glossary.ulcerative colitis: Inflammatory bowel disease of the colon; classically associated with episcleritis.
glossary.extra-articular: Affecting organs outside the joints in an arthritis such as RA.
glossary.Granulomatous: Inflammation with clusters of activated macrophages (granulomas).
glossary.T-cell mediated: Inflammation driven by T lymphocytes rather than antibodies.
glossary.immune complex: Antibody bound to antigen; can deposit in vessel walls and trigger inflammation.
glossary.ESR: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate; a non-specific marker of inflammation.
glossary.CRP: C-reactive protein; an acute-phase protein that rises with inflammation.
glossary.autoimmune screen: Blood tests for autoantibodies such as RF, anti-CCP, ANA and ANCA.
glossary.ANCA: Anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody; positive in small-vessel vasculitis such as GPA.
glossary.ANA: Antinuclear antibody; screening test for SLE and related diseases.
glossary.Anti-CCP: Antibody highly specific for rheumatoid arthritis.
glossary.Rheumatoid factor: Antibody against IgG found in most rheumatoid arthritis.
glossary.flurbiprofen: An oral NSAID used at 100 mg three times daily for mild scleritis.
glossary.NSAID: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug, e.g. ibuprofen; first systemic treatment for mild scleritis.
glossary.methylprednisolone: Potent corticosteroid given as pulsed IV doses for severe or necrotising scleritis.
glossary.prednisolone: Oral corticosteroid used for severe scleritis.
glossary.slit lamp: A microscope with a bright light used to examine the eye in detail.
glossary.visual acuity: Sharpness of vision, measured on a Snellen chart (e.g. 6/6).
glossary.conjunctivitis: Inflammation of the conjunctiva: gritty, red, with discharge, without deep pain.
glossary.anterior uveitis: Inflammation of the iris and ciliary body: photophobia, small pupil, ciliary flush.

technique.stem: A 54 year old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has a 5 day history of severe pain in her left eye. The pain is worse when she moves her eye and radiates to her jaw. The eye is deep red-violet and tender. Visual acuity is reduced. The redness does not blanch with topical phenylephrine.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question about a red eye: decide whether the pain is severe and where the inflammation is.

clues: worse when she moves her eye
does not blanch with topical phenylephrine
steps.x: RA is the classic association. Pain worse on eye movement, violet colour, tenderness and no blanching mean **deep scleral** inflammation.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Severe painful violet eye in RA that does not blanch: **scleritis**.

elim: Angle closure is sudden, with a fixed mid-dilated pupil, haloes and vomiting.
Uveitis gives photophobia and ciliary flush; pain is not typically worse on eye movement or radiating to the jaw.
Conjunctivitis is gritty with discharge and no deep pain.
Episcleritis is mild, not worse on movement and **blanches** with phenylephrine.

steps.x: **E. Scleritis.** Rule: RA + severe pain worse on movement + no blanching = scleritis.

technique.stem: A 61 year old man with granulomatosis with polyangiitis has a 3 day history of a severely painful red right eye that is worse on eye movement. He saw his GP this morning. The eye is violet and tender, and his vision is reduced to 6/18.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
o: Topical steroid trial and GP review

steps.x: Next step in a suspected scleritis: this is about urgency, not a scan.
Vasculitis plus severe pain on movement and a violet eye: **scleritis**. Reduced vision makes it sight-threatening.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Scleritis is an **ophthalmological emergency**: same-day ophthalmology.

elim: CT orbits is for orbital cellulitis or trauma; it does not diagnose scleritis.
Routine referral is too slow for a sight-threatening emergency.
A swab is for infective conjunctivitis with discharge.
GPs should not start topical steroids for a red eye; it delays specialist care.

steps.x: **C. Same-day ophthalmology assessment.** Rule: suspected scleritis is seen by eye casualty today.

technique.stem: A 48 year old woman with SLE has diffuse anterior scleritis confirmed by an ophthalmologist. There is no scleral thinning or necrosis. Her pain is moderate. She has no history of peptic ulcer disease and her renal function is normal.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial treatment?

steps.x: Initial treatment once scleritis is confirmed: decide mild or severe.

clues: no history of peptic ulcer disease
steps.x: No necrosis and moderate pain = **milder** disease. No ulcer and normal kidneys mean an NSAID is safe.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Mild scleritis: **systemic NSAID** such as flurbiprofen 100 mg orally TDS.

elim: Pulsed IV methylprednisolone is for severe or necrotising disease.
Rituximab is an IV specialist immunosuppressant for refractory disease, not first-line, and is not oral.
Chloramphenicol treats bacterial conjunctivitis.
Phenylephrine is a diagnostic test, not a treatment.

steps.x: **B. Oral flurbiprofen.** Rule: mild = oral NSAID; severe = systemic steroid.

technique.stem: A 66 year old woman with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis has scleritis. On slit lamp examination there is an area of bluish, thinned sclera through which the underlying choroid can be seen.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of the scleral thinning?
o: Collagen breakdown from raised intraocular pressure
Immune complex vasculitis causing ischaemic necrosis

steps.x: A mechanism question: link RA to the thinned sclera.
Long-standing RA plus thin blue sclera = **scleromalacia** from necrotising scleritis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Immune complex deposition and vasculitis cause **ischaemia and necrosis** of the sclera.

elim: Raised pressure does not cause focal scleral necrosis.
This is autoimmune, not infective.
Steroids treat the necrosis; they are not the cause in this vignette.
Topical NSAIDs are not the mechanism of RA scleromalacia.

steps.x: **B. Immune complex vasculitis causing ischaemic necrosis.** Rule: RA → vasculitis → necrosis → scleromalacia → rupture.

practice.stem: A 57 year old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has a 4 day history of a severe, boring pain in her right eye that woke her from sleep. The pain is worse on looking around and spreads to her cheek. The eye is diffusely deep red with a violet hue and is tender to touch. Her temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 84 bpm and BP 132/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: Most likely diagnosis of a painful red eye.
Severe pain that wakes her, worse on eye movement, violet hue and tenderness in RA.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Scleritis**.

elim: Angle closure has a fixed mid-dilated pupil, haloes and vomiting; pain is not worse on movement.
Uveitis gives photophobia, a small pupil and ciliary flush; pain does not radiate to the face or worsen on movement.
Conjunctivitis has discharge and grittiness, no deep pain.
Episcleritis is mild and not worse on movement.

steps.x: **E. Scleritis.** Rule: severe pain worse on eye movement in RA = scleritis.

practice.e: Severe, night-waking pain worse on eye movement with a violet tender eye in RA is scleritis. Episcleritis is mild and not worse on movement.

practice.stem: A 45 year old man has a painful red left eye for 2 days. He has a 6 month history of nasal crusting, epistaxis and haemoptysis. The pain is severe and worse on eye movement. The eye is violet and does not blanch with phenylephrine drops. His temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 92 bpm and BP 148/90 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: Diagnosis of a red eye in a man with a systemic illness.
Nasal crusting, epistaxis and haemoptysis suggest **GPA (vasculitis)**. Severe pain on movement and no blanching = deep scleral inflammation.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Vasculitis-associated **scleritis**.

elim: Angle closure is sudden with a fixed mid-dilated pupil, haloes and vomiting.
Uveitis gives photophobia, a small pupil and ciliary flush; it fits no vasculitis-violet-eye picture as well.
Episcleritis blanches with phenylephrine and is mild.
Orbital cellulitis gives proptosis, lid swelling and fever, often after sinusitis.

steps.x: **E. Scleritis.** Rule: vasculitis clues + non-blanching violet eye = scleritis.

practice.e: Upper and lower airway features suggest GPA, a classic cause of scleritis. Episcleritis would blanch with phenylephrine.

practice.stem: A 50 year old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has a painful red eye. An ophthalmology registrar is asked to distinguish scleritis from episcleritis at the bedside and instils topical phenylephrine 10%.

steps.x: Most likely finding with phenylephrine in scleritis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The deep redness **persists** (no blanching).

elim: Blanching is the finding in episcleritis.
Fluorescein staining shows a corneal abrasion or ulcer.
A fixed mid-dilated pupil is angle closure glaucoma.
Discharge suggests bacterial conjunctivitis.

steps.x: **D. Persistence of the deep redness.** Rule: no blanching = scleritis.

practice.e: Phenylephrine blanches superficial episcleral vessels but not the deep scleral plexus, so scleritis redness persists.

practice.stem: A 39 year old woman has a 7 day history of a severely painful, red right eye that is tender and worse on eye movement. She also has a malar rash, mouth ulcers and painful swollen fingers.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: This asks for the diagnosis that explains both the eye and the systemic picture.

clues: malar rash, mouth ulcers and painful swollen fingers
steps.x: Severe pain worse on movement = **scleritis**. Malar rash, mouth ulcers and arthritis = **SLE**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Scleritis secondary to SLE**.

elim: Episcleritis is mild and not worse on movement; Crohn's would give bowel symptoms.
Shingles gives a dermatomal vesicular rash on the forehead.
Reactive arthritis gives conjunctivitis and urethritis after infection, without a malar rash.
Sarcoid uveitis has no malar rash and pain is not worse on movement.

steps.x: **D. Scleritis secondary to SLE.** Rule: severe pain on movement + autoimmune multisystem disease = scleritis.

practice.e: Severe pain worse on eye movement with SLE features (malar rash, mouth ulcers, arthritis) is SLE-associated scleritis. Episcleritis is mild.

practice.stem: A 71 year old woman with 30 years of rheumatoid arthritis has had scleritis for several months. Her pain has worsened despite oral NSAIDs. On examination there is a bluish area of thinned sclera. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 78 bpm and BP 138/76 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most serious complication she is at risk of?

steps.x: Most serious complication of this scleritis.
Long-standing RA with a thin blue sclera = **scleromalacia**, from necrotising scleritis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Thinning can progress to **globe rupture**.

elim: Cataract can follow chronic steroids but is not the most serious risk here.
Ptosis is not a complication of scleritis.
Retinal vein occlusion is linked to hypertension and glaucoma, not scleral thinning.
Subconjunctival haemorrhage is benign.

steps.x: **B. Globe rupture.** Rule: scleritis → thinning (scleromalacia) → rarely rupture.

practice.e: Scleral thinning in necrotising RA scleritis can progress to globe rupture. The other options are not the feared complication.

practice.stem: A 63 year old man with granulomatosis with polyangiitis has necrotising scleritis of the left eye. There is an avascular area of sclera and his vision has fallen to 6/36. His pain is not controlled by oral NSAIDs. His temperature is 37.1°C, pulse rate 88 bpm and BP 142/84 mmHg.

practice.e: Severe necrotising scleritis needs systemic steroids, often pulsed IV methylprednisolone, with immunosuppressants for the underlying vasculitis.

practice.stem: A 58 year old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has recurrent scleritis. Each episode has needed oral prednisolone, and symptoms return when the dose is reduced below 15 mg daily. Her rheumatoid arthritis is also active.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

steps.x: **B. Immunosuppressant under specialist care.** Rule: underlying autoimmune disease = specialist immunosuppression.

practice.e: When scleritis is driven by active autoimmune disease and is steroid-dependent, specialist immunosuppression (e.g. methotrexate, rituximab) is added.

practice.stem: A 47 year old woman has a severely painful red eye that is worse on eye movement. Topical phenylephrine 10% is instilled and, after 15 minutes, the deep red-violet colour is unchanged.
practice.q: Which is the most likely explanation for this finding?
o: Inflammation of the deep scleral vascular plexus

steps.x: Explain the failed blanching (mechanism).
Severe pain on movement + no blanching = scleritis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Scleritis involves the **deeper vascular plexus**, which phenylephrine does not constrict.

elim: Conjunctival vessels are superficial and would blanch.
Phenylephrine is an alpha-agonist and constricts vessels.
Raised pressure is glaucoma and does not explain non-blanching.
Subconjunctival haemorrhage is painless and bright red, not a violet, painful eye.

steps.x: **B. Deep scleral plexus inflammation.** Rule: superficial vessels blanch; deep vessels do not.

practice.e: Phenylephrine constricts superficial (episcleral/conjunctival) vessels; scleritis involves the deep vascular plexus, so redness persists.
